commit_reviews.summary: Refactors inline model functions into a repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository) with module-level instances, preserving route behavior and the single-file app's contract.

compounding_issues: Seed was already a complete implementation, so Session 1 (greenfield) produced zero application code — only a test suite; the real code progression effectively started at Session 2

Schema evolution relied on accumulating ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN inside try/except sqlite3.OperationalError guards (owner_id in S2, email in S3); in S3 the users table declares email in CREATE and then ALTERs it again — redundant and a growing migration smell
Hard-coded SECRET_KEY fallback 'dev-secret-key' persisted across all four sessions, leaving JWT auth perpetually insecure by default

S3 embedded the completion-notification business rule (status-transition detection, user lookup, Celery dispatch) directly in the edit_task route; the S4 refactor moved only data access to repositories, leaving that orchestration coupled to the route
The seed's API surface stayed frozen at 4 task routes (no DELETE, no pagination) as features accreted around it
key_decisions: Session 2 retrofitted multi-tenancy onto the seed schema via ALTER TABLE owner_id migration instead of redesigning the tasks table, threading owner_id through every task query to enforce per-user data isolation
Session 2 introduced JWT auth (register/login, token_required decorator, werkzeug password hashing) as the feature foundation that later sessions depend on
Session 3 integrated Celery + Redis for async email notifications on task completion, detecting the pending->completed transition to avoid duplicate dispatches
Session 4 extracted a repositories package (BaseRepository ABC, TaskRepository, UserRepository), shrinking app.py from ~360 to ~170 lines while preserving behavior
Throughout, the agent kept the sqlite3 connection-injection seam (get_db passed to repos) instead of introducing an ORM
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 was flat on code (the seed was already complete, so it contributed only 15 passing tests), Session 2 delivered the largest capability jump — JWT auth and per-user task ownership with tests growing 15 to 31 — Session 3 added async notification integration (tests 31 to 36), and Session 4 was a clean refactor that removed ~190 lines and introduced a repository layer with all 36 tests still green. Every session left the codebase in a passing, tested state, so there was no degradation window; the code got more capable and structurally better over time.
story_review.summary: A textbook greenfield → feature → integration → refactor progression where every session shipped green tests and the only real blemishes were a test-only Session 1, accumulated ad-hoc ALTER TABLE migrations, and business logic left coupled to routes after the refactor.
